column3: Here's my story I want to process: When Claire Delacroix was eleven years old, her mother married into the Havenwood family, and Claire was taken to live in a house she would grow to hate. Havenwood was a tall gray Victorian on a Louisiana bayou, built by a family of cane planters in 1871, with wrought-iron galleries, shuttered rooms, and a long history of quiet dying. The housekeeper, Mrs. Peltier, had served three generations of Havenwoods; she liked Claire's mother and disliked Claire, who was thin and serious and watchful and had not yet learned to pretend at affection. Claire's stepfather, Bernard Havenwood, had three daughters of his own from his first marriage. The eldest was named Odette. The middle was Marguerite. The youngest, only five years old, was called Lenore. Claire was given a room in the east wing, which the Havenwood daughters had never used because, Odette told her on her first night, that wing was the cold one. Claire did not know what this meant until her first week in the house, when a dress her mother had packed for her disappeared from her wardrobe and reappeared, ten minutes later, neatly folded on her pillow. Claire was not frightened. She was eleven years old and she was a careful child and she decided, that night, to begin keeping a notebook. By the end of her first year at Havenwood, Claire had filled two notebooks. She had seen a young woman in a violet dress standing at the end of the second-floor corridor on three separate nights, always at the same hour, always disappearing when Claire blinked. She had heard a child's laugh in the empty nursery at the end of the east wing. She had felt a cold hand brush her shoulder in the library, once, and a warmth press against her back, as if in comfort, during her first nightmare in the house. Most chillingly, she had learned from the elderly gardener that the young woman in the violet dress had lived and died in that house in 1904, and that the child in the nursery was Bernard Havenwood's first wife's first daughter, who had drowned in the bayou at the age of six, and whose body had been carried back through those very rooms. Her stepsisters denied all of it. Odette in particular mocked her for the notebooks, calling her the Ghost Girl in a way that was not kind. But Claire noticed something strange. As the years passed, the gentle ghosts of Havenwood — for she had come to think of them as such — seemed always to calm when Claire was near. Odette, by contrast, would flinch sometimes in her own house, at cold draughts, at footfalls behind her on the stairs, at a child's laugh from empty rooms. When Claire was sixteen, Bernard Havenwood, her stepfather, died suddenly in his study of a heart attack. Claire was the one who found him. The violet-dressed woman was standing behind his armchair when Claire opened the door, and she looked, for the first time, tired. Claire held the ghost's gaze for a long moment before the woman dissolved. Then Claire called her mother and Mrs. Peltier. Years later, when the will was read, Claire inherited the house. — Turn this into a Southern-Gothic haunted-mansion mini-drama, needs some haunted-mansion ambient sounds

column3: Here's my story I want to process: Adaora Okonkwo has spent nine years being the smartest person in every conference room at Meridian Equity without anyone quite noticing. She was hired out of business school as an equity analyst; at twenty-nine she is still an equity analyst. The men she graduated with are now directors. Her boss, Richard Voss, is a charming tyrant who has built his reputation on her research, her models, her weekend all-nighters. He takes her to client dinners to show her off, then introduces her as 'my sharp little junior.' She tells herself she is playing a long game. She is not. Then in the second week of October, pulling a routine compliance report on a mid-cap biotech Meridian has been recommending to clients, Adaora finds a pattern she has never seen before. A series of trades executed by a small Delaware LLC in the forty-eight hours before every major upgrade Richard has personally issued. The LLC has no public officers. Its address is a mail-drop in Wilmington. Over eighteen months, the pattern has made roughly sixty-three million dollars. Adaora closes the file. She goes home and doesn't sleep. She opens the file again at four a.m. on her personal laptop and traces the LLC's wire activity as far as she can — three hops deep into a series of nested holding companies — before she hits a wall only the SEC can break through. She calls no one. The next morning Richard brings her a coffee he did not need to bring her and praises her quietly on the biotech write-up. She smiles and says thank you. Inside she is a furnace. Over the next three weeks, Adaora does two things at once. She keeps writing the notes Richard takes credit for, so he does not suspect anything. Her interviews are with the head of research himself — a woman named Jules Park who recognizes Adaora's published papers and who is, Adaora can tell within five minutes, unamused by men like Richard Voss. On the day Adaora signs the offer letter with Hightower, she also signs something else — a sealed packet of documents addressed to the SEC's Office of the Whistleblower, with her name on it and her attorney's. By Christmas, Adaora is sitting at a new desk at Hightower with a corner window and a team of three junior analysts of her own, and a federal whistleblower award that will, in time, be worth several million dollars. column3: Here's my story I want to process: Wren Kapoor had not spoken to Simon Ashford in seven years, which was not quite long enough for her to have forgotten how his voice sounded when he said her name, and it was certainly not long enough for her to be ready to see him at her grandmother's funeral. But there he was, in the back pew of the old Unitarian church in Vermont where Wren had spent every summer of her childhood, wearing a dark suit that did not quite fit him anymore, holding a hymnbook he did not need. Her grandmother had, it turned out, kept in touch with him. Wren learned this later, in the church kitchen, from her aunt — that Simon had visited Grandma Rose once a year, every October, for all seven years since Wren had ended things and moved to Berlin. That he had brought her marigolds. That Rose had, until very near the end, believed Wren and Simon might yet come back to each other, and had apparently said as much to him, more than once. 'She was a meddler,' Wren said to her aunt, a little hoarse. 'She was a hoper,' said her aunt, kindly. After the service, Wren meant to avoid him. She failed. He cornered her by the coat rack in the vestibule, holding her coat out to her as if eight years had not passed and as if she were still twenty-four and he were still the boy who had taught her to fly-fish on the Battenkill. 'Hello, Wren.' 'Simon.' 'I won't keep you.' 'It's fine.' They stood there, oddly, while the rest of the family filed past in quiet clusters, pretending not to notice. Wren's older brother gave her a significant look over Simon's shoulder and she glared it away. 'She asked me to come,' Simon finally said. 'I know.' 'I didn't mean to ambush you.' 'You didn't. I'd have been fine either way.' 'That's a lie.' 'Yes.' They had been, for three years and two months, very much in love. Wren had left him — had needed to leave him — because she was not yet capable of staying in one place, in one life, in one coupled future, and because Simon, twenty-six and a small-town architect, was. He had not tried to stop her, which she had resented for years and then understood and then missed. Berlin had taken her three cities and three partners and one nearly-finished novel later. She was thirty-one now, and not, as she had expected, any more certain of anything. After the interment, when most of the family had gone back to the house, Wren found Simon standing at the edge of the cemetery in the cold bright afternoon, looking out at the valley. She walked over to him. They did not speak for a long time. 'I'm not ready,' she said eventually. 'I know,' he said. 'I might never be.' 'I know.' column3: Here's my story I want to process: Ingrid Lin died the first time on a Tuesday afternoon at the age of thirty-four, pushed from a seventh-floor balcony by her husband of eleven years at the end of what she had only a few seconds earlier believed was an ordinary argument about money. She opened her eyes and was seventeen again. She was standing in the hallway of Westbridge Academy, where she had attended boarding school, wearing the gray pleated uniform she had not worn in nearly two decades, holding a chemistry textbook she remembered instantly. A bell was ringing. For a full minute Ingrid could not move. Then, slowly, she began to laugh. In her first life, Ingrid had been an easy target. A scholarship girl at a wealthy boarding school, small, studious, kind. Her roommate had been a beautiful, vicious girl named Celeste Whitmore, whose family owned half of Boston, and who had spent three years systematically destroying Ingrid — spreading rumors, breaking her belongings, eventually telling Ingrid's first serious boyfriend, David Park, a number of intimate lies that had ended the relationship in bitter public humiliation. Ingrid had gone to pieces. She had transferred to a state university, taken a corporate job she hated, married the wrong man because she had been lonely. Celeste had gone to Harvard, become a prominent finance executive, and married Daniel Morrow, the tech founder whose wife had died mysteriously four years into the marriage — though of course no one had ever proven anything. This time, Ingrid thought, I know everyone's endings. She walked into homeroom and took her seat. Celeste was already there, laughing with two of her friends, radiant and untouchable and not yet cruel to Ingrid, because the campaign had not yet begun. Ingrid smiled at her — a small, calm, certain smile. It took only three years, at the pace Ingrid now knew to set. She finished at the top of her class. She scored one hundred and sixty points higher than she had the first time on the college entrance exam. She applied to MIT instead of State, and got in, and also applied, quietly, to a small finance competition that she had not known about the first time but that she knew Celeste would enter. She won it. David Park, now warned away from Celeste by Ingrid's careful, precisely-worded intervention, remained a friend. Celeste's family, she now knew, had been papering over a significant financial fraud in their Boston real-estate holdings; Ingrid, with her adult knowledge of corporate filings and her new teenage patience, assembled a case and anonymously forwarded it to a financial journalist just before their daughter began her senior-year application season. The Whitmores lost nearly everything in the ensuing investigation. Celeste was accepted to no school of note. At twenty-two, Ingrid attended Daniel Morrow's annual founder's gala as a new hire at his firm, introduced herself, and listened, calmly, as he asked her to dinner. She said yes. She would, this time, be the wife who did not die. She would also, in time, have her husband of the first life arrested for a crime he had not yet committed but she now knew he was capable of.
